title: Ibn Battuta
hook: the traveler from Tangier who set out for Mecca and kept going

segments.voice: Yesterday, the madrasah: Nizam al-Mulk's endowed colleges, and al-Ghazali leaving his chair in Baghdad. Your line was: a college in every city. Did you support a school, or thank a teacher? Day nine hundred fifty.

Tangier, on the northern tip of Morocco. A young man is leaving it for Mecca, to make the pilgrimage. In his own telling, he goes alone, with no companion and no caravan to join, and parting from his parents weighs on him, and on them. He's a student of law. He plans to come home. Instead, the road keeps opening. Egypt, Syria, Mecca, and then on, east and south and east again, for years, until the book of his travels reads like a map of a great stretch of the Muslim world of his time, and some lands beyond it. Today: Ibn Battuta.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN LEAVES TANGIER.` → `ALONE, FOR MECCA.` → `THE ROAD KEEPS OPENING.`

segments.voice: His book is called the Rihla, which simply means the journey. He didn't write it with his own pen. Back home at last in Morocco, he told his story aloud, and a court scholar named Ibn Juzayy wrote it down and polished it. So what we read is a traveler's memory, shaped by an editor. Historians have questioned some passages, wondering whether he really reached every place he describes. That's worth knowing. The book is still a marvel. What kept him moving? Part of it was the pilgrimage. Part of it was that a man trained in Islamic law could find work almost anywhere the law was used. In one land he serves as a judge. In another he is a guest of a sultan, then out of favor, then on the road again. He prays in mosques he's never seen, eats at the tables of strangers, stays in lodges kept by Sufis for travelers. The world he walks through shares a language of prayer, a law and a habit of hospitality, even when everything else changes. One verse of the Qur'an tells its hearers to go and look. In Pickthall's translation: "Travel in the land and see how He originated creation." For Ibn Battuta, the journey was not only distance. It was attention: to food, to customs, to scholars, to the strangeness and sameness of people. When he finally sat down to tell it all, much of what he described was other people: what they ate, how they prayed, how they treated a stranger at the door. The traveler.
screen: `THE RIHLA — THE JOURNEY.` · `TOLD ALOUD, WRITTEN BY ANOTHER.` · `A JUDGE, A GUEST, A WANDERER.` · `TRAVEL IN THE LAND AND SEE.` · then, large: `THE TRAVELER.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at a place as a traveler. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind somewhere near you that you have never actually been. A street you always drive past. A shop you never enter. A park on the other side of town. A mosque, a church or a temple you have only seen from outside. Picture walking into it as Ibn Battuta might have, ready to notice: what people eat there, how they greet each other, what they're proud of. If you pray, you can ask to see it with open eyes. If you don't, simply choose the place. Later today, or this week, go. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Battuta. The traveler from Tangier who set out for Mecca and kept going, and whose spoken memories became the Rihla, the journey. Today's word.
Your line: the traveler. Today, go somewhere new, even if it's only around the corner, and notice one thing the way a traveler would. Day nine hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Ibn Battuta's Rihla is read today as a travel book and a window on the Muslim world of his time, and pilgrims still set out for Mecca to perform the Hajj.
